desc:
A matrix mat contains only 0s and 1s, and at least one 0. For every cell, find the distance to the closest cell holding 0, where moving to a cell that shares a side (up, down, left or right) counts as one step. Cells are not blocked in any way.

Return a matrix of the same shape with these distances.

mat = [[0,0,0],
       [0,1,0],
       [1,1,1]]

result = [[0,0,0],
          [0,1,0],
          [1,2,1]]
hints: A brute force that scans the whole matrix for the nearest zero from every cell is O((rows × cols)<sup>2</sup>). Try to share work between cells.
Searching from the zeros is better than searching to them. What if all zeros were the starting points of a single BFS?

Seed the queue with every zero at distance 0. When you take a cell from the queue, each unvisited neighbour gets the cell's distance plus one. The first time a cell is reached is its smallest distance.
editorial: Start a BFS whose queue initially contains every cell with value 0 (distance 0); all other cells are marked as not yet reached. Pop a cell, and for each neighbour that has not been reached yet set its distance to the popped distance plus one and push it. BFS expands in rings of increasing distance around the whole set of zeros, so a cell is first reached along a shortest path to its nearest zero.

Every cell is queued once, giving O(rows × cols). A two-pass dynamic programming sweep also works: one pass from the top-left taking the minimum of the upper and left neighbours plus one, then one pass from the bottom-right using the lower and right neighbours.
